submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on running legal and institutional boilerplate -- the formulaic clauses of software licences, copyright and warranty notices, contracts, statutes, regulations, and case/patent boilerplate -- and inside such a clause it is active on most of the clause at once rather than on one word, with the peak on the connective that glues the formula ('agreed to in writing' 8.3 on ' in'; 'non-transferable right to' 5.7 on ' to'; 'in any form or by any means' 5.3 on ' now'; 'Unless required by applicable law' 5.5/5.2 on ' Unless'/' required'; 'Licensed under the Apache License' 5.2 on ' Licensed'; 'not reasonably arguable' 4.6 on ' reasonably'). It falls to near zero on narrative, news, fiction, recipe, chat, academic and technical prose and on legal vocabulary dropped into an ordinary sentence ('The lawyer read the contract' 0.2; 'He put the offer in writing' 0.4 versus 'must be made in writing' 4.8), so the driver is the formula and register, not the word list; the same neuron's positive pole is complementary (it peaks on the opening piece of a rare word, ' ke' in Inverkeithing 8.7 where this pole reads 0.00, and is ~0 on licence clauses), while two weaker 1-3 responses sit outside the claim: subword pieces of rare or foreign words (' Ker' in Kerboua 5.1, ' Yak' in Yakutumba 3.3, 'In' in MacInnes 2.5, kana inside Japanese words 6.4) and the punctuation/attribute glue of code and markup ('="' 3.8, a CSS declaration ':' 3.1, '=-' in a Gradle property 4.1).

namespace Doctrine\ORM\Internal\Hydration;

use Doctrine\DBAL\Connection;

/**
 * Hydrator that produces flat, rectangular results of scalar data.
 * The created result is almost the same as a regular SQL result set, except
 * that column names are mapped to field names and data type conversions take place.
 *
 * @author Roman Borschel <roman@code-factory.org>
 * @since 2.0
 */
class ScalarHydrator extends AbstractHydrator
{
    /** @override */
    protected function _hydrateAll()
    {
        $result = array();
        $cache = array();
        while ($data = $this->_stmt->fetch(\PDO::FETCH_ASSOC)) {
            $result[] = $this->_gatherScalarRowData($data, $cache);
        }
        return $result;
    }

    /** @override */
    protected function _hydrateRow(array $data, array &$cache, array &$result)
    {
        $result[] = $this->_gatherScalarRowData($data, $cache);
    }
}

From 1 July 2018, the Tax Office is advising Australians that if they find an error in their tax return or activity statement they will not incur a penalty but will advise of the error and how to get it right next time.

Penalty relief will only apply to eligible taxpayers or entities (i.e., turnover of less than $10 million) every three years.

Eligible individuals will only be given penalty relief on their tax return or activity statement if they make an inadvertent error because they either:
– took a position on income tax that is not reasonably arguable, or
– failed to take reasonable care

The ATO will not provide penalty relief when individuals have (in the past three years):
Received penalty relief
– Avoided tax payment or committed fraud
– Accrued taxation debts with no intention of being able to pay (i.e., phoenix activity)
– Previously penalised for reckless or intentional disregard of the law
– Participated in the management or control of another entity which has evaded tax.

Individuals can not apply for penalty relief. The ATO is reminding individuals that they will provide relief during an audit should it apply.

Penalty relief will not be applied to:
– Wealthy individuals and their businesses
– Associates of wealthy individuals (that may be deemed a small business entity in their own right)
– Public groups, significant global entities and associates

Penalty relief will also not be applied to certain taxes, i.e., fringe benefits tax (FBT) or super guarantee (SG).

Most organisms rely on an innate immune system as their first line of defense against infection. Within the innate immune system, the Toll-like receptors (TLRs), a family of evolutionarily ancient receptors found on the surface of many cell types, are critical for pathogen recognition outside the cell. About 12 TLRs recognize structures specific to pathogens, such as bacterial cell wall components, bacterial filament proteins, or certain types of nucleic acid. This recognition event initiates a signal inside the cell, which induces the rapid secretion of antimicrobial and inflammatory proteins. Inside the cell, the NOD proteins and RNA helicases such as MDA5 recognize similar pathogen-associated structures to those recognized by TLRs. Remarkably, given the structural diversity of the structures that they recognize, all TLRs and NODs rely on a "leucine-rich repeat" (LRR) domain to recognize pathogen-associated structures. The overall goal of our research program on innate immune sensors is to understand how they recognize conserved molecular patterns in pathogens, and how this recognition is translated into an innate immune response. Our structural approach will provide unique insights into these important processes. First, we aim to determine the structure of one or more TLR-ligand complexes, by X-ray crystallography. Alternative crystallization targets are NOD-ligand or helicase-RNA complexes. We propose to use novel protein expression techniques to maximize protein yields. Our structures will likely define novel principles of molecular recognition. By revealing the conformational changes associated with ligand binding, the structures will provide insight on how pathogen recognition is translated into a signal in the cell that elicits an immune response. Our work will also guide efforts to design synthetic agonists or antagonists with immunomodulatory properties. Such compounds would have a wide range of medical applications, particularly as vaccine adjuvants or anti-inflammatory therapeutics.

abstract: |
    We give a general construction of debiased/locally robust/orthogonal (LR) moment functions for GMM, where the derivative with respect to first step nonparametric estimation is zero and equivalently first step estimation has no effect on the influence function. This construction consists of adding an estimator of the influence function adjustment term for first step nonparametric estimation to identifying or original moment conditions. We also give numerical methods for estimating LR moment functions that do not require an explicit formula for the adjustment term.

    LR moment conditions have reduced bias and so are important when the first step is machine learning. We derive LR moment conditions for dynamic discrete choice based on first step machine learning estimators of conditional choice probabilities.

    We provide simple and general asymptotic theory for LR estimators based on sample splitting. This theory uses the additive decomposition of LR moment conditions into an identifying condition and a first step influence adjustment. Our conditions require only mean square consistency and a few (generally either one or two) readily interpretable rate conditions.

    LR moment functions have the advantage of being less sensitive to first step estimation. Some LR moment functions are also doubly robust meaning they hold if one first step is incorrect. I had assumed the flat would take a weekend. It took three. My father had kept every piece of paper that ever crossed his desk, and the desk itself had gone to the charity shop on the first afternoon, so the paper had nowhere left to live.

On Saturday morning my sister and I carried the filing boxes out to the landing and sat on the stairs with tea, dividing the contents into three piles: keep, bin, ask someone. The keep pile was small at first. Photographs of people neither of us could name. His passport, expired in 2011. A postcard from a town on the coast that he had never mentioned and that I later found, after a long search, to be somewhere in Northumberland.

By lunchtime we had reached the kitchen drawer, the one that had never opened properly. Inside were manuals for a washing machine we had sold in 2009, a warranty for a kettle, and a bundle of receipts held together with a rubber band so perished that it crumbled when my sister touched it. She laughed, and the laugh turned into something else, and we sat on the floor for a while without saying anything, listening to the neighbour's radio through the wall.

The sitting room took longer because the sitting room contained the books. He had arranged them by nothing either of us could work out. A dictionary of saints beside a guide to plumbing; a history of the Bosphorus beside a self-help book with a torn cover and no author's name. My sister took the novels and I took everything with an index, and we decided to sort the rest later, which is what we had said in the hospital corridor, and which had turned out to mean never.

On Sunday I took the upstairs bedroom alone. The wardrobe was empty except for three coats and a shoebox labelled, in his small backward-slanting hand, DO NOT THROW. Inside the box were bank statements, an insurance schedule for a car he had sold long before the statements were printed, and a brown envelope with a solicitor's stamp on the corner but no letter inside. I put the envelope on the bed and went to make tea and came back and did not open it.

The letter that mattered was in the drawer of the small desk we had kept, the one nobody was meant to use. It was a copy of a lease, dated nearly forty years earlier, for the flat he had rented before I was born. The paper had gone the colour of weak tea. The signature at the bottom was his, younger and more careful, and below it, underlined twice, was the clause I read aloud to my sister over the phone because she had gone to get sandwiches:

'The Tenant shall not assign or underlet the whole or any part of the Premises without the prior written consent of the Landlord, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld, and shall not permit any person other than the Tenant to occupy the Premises for more than fourteen consecutive days.'

There was more, a second page of it, clauses about repairs and notices and the deposit, and a schedule at the back listing the furniture that had come with the flat. My sister was quiet when I finished. Then she said that he had asked the landlord to change that clause in 1982, that he had told her this once in the car, and that the landlord had refused, and that he had gone on living happily in the flat for another eleven years anyway, because rules that were never enforced were, in his view, a kind of decoration.

That was the whole of him, I thought, or as much of him as could be put in a shoebox: a man who kept the paperwork of every decision he had ever hesitated over, and who had been, in the end, entirely content to disobey the rules that nobody was counting.

explanation_scores.explanation: The negative pole fires on running legal and institutional boilerplate -- the formulaic clauses of software licences, copyright and warranty notices, contracts, statutes, regulations, and case/patent boilerplate -- and inside such a clause it is active on most of the clause at once rather than on one word, with the peak on the connective that glues the formula ('agreed to in writing' 8.3 on ' in'; 'non-transferable right to' 5.7 on ' to'; 'in any form or by any means' 5.3 on ' now'; 'Unless required by applicable law' 5.5/5.2 on ' Unless'/' required'; 'Licensed under the Apache License' 5.2 on ' Licensed'; 'not reasonably arguable' 4.6 on ' reasonably'). It falls to near zero on narrative, news, fiction, recipe, chat, academic and technical prose and on legal vocabulary dropped into an ordinary sentence ('The lawyer read the contract' 0.2; 'He put the offer in writing' 0.4 versus 'must be made in writing' 4.8), so the driver is the formula and register, not the word list; the same neuron's positive pole is complementary (it peaks on the opening piece of a rare word, ' ke' in Inverkeithing 8.7 where this pole reads 0.00, and is ~0 on licence clauses), while two weaker 1-3 responses sit outside the claim: subword pieces of rare or foreign words (' Ker' in Kerboua 5.1, ' Yak' in Yakutumba 3.3, 'In' in MacInnes 2.5, kana inside Japanese words 6.4) and the punctuation/attribute glue of code and markup ('="' 3.8, a CSS declaration ':' 3.1, '=-' in a Gradle property 4.1).
